title: YOU CALL HIM LORD… BUT WHAT IF JESUS SAYS, “I NEVER KNEW YOU”?
paragraphs: YOU CALL HIM LORD… BUT WHAT IF JESUS SAYS, “I NEVER KNEW YOU”?

The terrifying difference between believing Jesus is real and truly belonging to Him—and why Romans 10:9, Luke 6:46, and James 2:19 may expose the most dangerous misunderstanding in modern Christianity.
There is a kind of person who believes Jesus is the Son of God, believes He died on the cross, believes He rose from the dead, and believes that one day He will return.
And yet, there is a question that should make every professing Christian examine their heart.
What if everything you say about Jesus is correct… but your relationship with Him is not?
What if your theology sounds Christian, your social media looks Christian, your vocabulary is Christian, but your heart has quietly refused the very Lord you claim to worship?
Imagine standing before Jesus Christ, expecting to hear, “Well done.”
You remember the prayers you prayed. The sermons you heard. The Bible verses you memorized. The religious conversations you participated in.
You are confident because you have always believed in Him.
Then you remember the words Jesus spoke in Matthew 7:21:
“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.” (KJV)
And suddenly, a question you spent your whole life avoiding becomes impossible to ignore.
Did I actually follow Jesus, or did I merely agree that He was Lord?
This is not a question designed to rob genuine believers of their assurance.
It is a question designed to expose false assurance before eternity makes the truth impossible to escape.
Because the Gospel does not invite us merely to acknowledge Jesus.
It calls us to trust Him.
And the Jesus who saves sinners is also the Lord who transforms them.
There is a difference.
An eternal difference.
The apostle Paul writes in Romans 10:9:
Read that promise carefully.
It is breathtaking.
Salvation is not presented as a prize reserved for people who have successfully repaired their entire lives.
Paul does not say you must first become morally flawless, overcome every temptation, erase every sinful memory, or achieve a particular level of religious performance.
He points us to Jesus Christ—crucified, risen, and confessed as Lord.
But something extraordinary happens when we examine Paul's original Greek.
The expression translated “Lord Jesus” includes the words:
Κύριον Ἰησοῦν — Kyrion Iēsoun.
Jesus as Lord.

The Greek word κύριος (kyrios) means lord, master, or one possessing authority. Its precise force depends on context, but throughout the New Testament it carries profound significance when applied to Jesus.
Paul is not introducing a powerless religious figure whom we may admire while permanently reserving ultimate authority for ourselves.
He is proclaiming the risen Lord.
And the confession of Romans 10:9 is not meant to be detached from genuine faith.
The Greek verb πιστεύσῃς (pisteusēs), translated “believe,” comes from pisteuō, meaning to believe or trust.
Paul speaks of believing “in thine heart.”
In the biblical understanding, the heart is not merely the place where emotions happen. It is deeply connected with a person's inner life, convictions, desires, and will.
This is not an invitation to pronounce a religious sentence while deliberately rejecting the One whom that sentence identifies.
It is a promise of salvation through genuine faith in the risen Christ.
And Romans 10:13 makes the invitation even more beautiful:
“For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.”
Whosoever.
The ashamed.
The addicted.
The religious hypocrite finally admitting the truth.
The person who has fallen so many times that getting up feels almost dishonest.
The man who secretly wonders whether God could still forgive him.
The woman who cries after everyone else has gone to sleep because she knows the distance between the life she displays and the life she actually lives.
Whosoever calls upon the Lord.
But here is where we must be careful.
The Bible does not teach that salvation is earned through obedience. Neither does it teach that saving faith is a license to reject Christ's authority.
Those two errors have wounded countless souls.
One tells struggling Christians that they must perform well enough to deserve salvation.
The other tells unrepentant people that they can possess salvation while knowingly and permanently refusing the Savior.
Both distort the Gospel.
And Jesus Himself confronts the second error with a question so simple that it leaves us nowhere to hide.
In Luke 6:46, He asks:
“And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” (KJV)
Read it again.
Slowly.
Why do you call Me Lord…
And refuse to do what I say?
The Greek reads:
Τί δέ με καλεῖτε· Κύριε κύριε, καὶ οὐ ποιεῖτε ἃ λέγω;
Ti de me kaleite: Kyrie kyrie, kai ou poieite ha legō?
“Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?”
Notice what Jesus exposes.
Not a lack of religious vocabulary.
Not a failure to recognize His title.
But the contradiction between a person's confession and conduct.
They call Him Lord.
Yet their lives resist His words.
And immediately afterward, Jesus tells the story of two builders.
One hears His words and acts upon them. That person resembles a man who digs deeply and builds his house upon rock.
The other hears His words but does not act upon them. That person resembles a man who builds without a proper foundation.
When the flood comes, the difference becomes visible.
The storm does not create the foundation.
It reveals it.
And perhaps that is what makes this passage so unsettling.
Two people may hear the same sermons.
Attend the same church.
Know the same worship songs.
Post the same Christian quotations.
Yet beneath the surface, something may be radically different.
One is learning to surrender to Jesus.
The other is learning how to sound surrendered without actually yielding.
One struggles against sin and repeatedly returns to Christ.
The other makes peace with sin and expects Christ to make peace with it too.
One says, “Lord, I am weak. Help me obey You.”
The other says, “Lord, I know what You said, but I have already decided that I will not listen.”
Those are not the same spiritual condition.
And we must never confuse them.
Because there is a difference between a believer who falls while following Jesus and a person who has decided that following Jesus is unnecessary.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
He failed terribly.
He wept bitterly.
But his failure was not the end of his story.
The risen Jesus restored him.
John 21 records Christ's gracious encounter with Peter, including His renewed command:
Consider that.
Jesus did not tell Peter that his denial was harmless.
He did not pretend the betrayal had never happened.
But neither did He discard a broken disciple who returned to Him.
He restored him.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain in rebellion.
Grace that reaches into failure and calls a person forward again.
Perhaps you need to hear that today.
You have sinned.
You have compromised.
You have promised God things you did not keep.
You have gone back to habits you thought you had finally overcome.
And now, whenever someone preaches about obedience, your heart begins to panic.
You wonder whether every failure proves that you were never saved.
But listen carefully.
The presence of a struggle does not automatically prove the absence of saving faith.
The Christian life is not sinless perfection.
First John 1:8 warns that claiming to be without sin is self-deception.
And 1 John 2:1 offers this extraordinary encouragement:
“My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.” (KJV)
John does not encourage sin.
He points sinners to their Advocate.
Jesus Christ.
The righteous One.
Your hope is not that you will never stumble again.
Your hope is that the crucified and risen Savior is sufficient to forgive, restore, and sustain those who belong to Him.
But now we must confront another passage.
And this one may be even more disturbing.
James 2:19 says:
“Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble.” (KJV)
The demons believe.
Let that sink in.
They are not atheists.
They do not need convincing that the spiritual world exists.
They know God is real.
They recognize truths that human beings often deny.
And yet their knowledge does not constitute saving faith.
The Greek text says:
καὶ τὰ δαιμόνια πιστεύουσιν καὶ φρίσσουσιν
kai ta daimonia pisteuousin kai phrissousin.
“And even the demons believe—and shudder.”
The word φρίσσουσιν (phrissousin) conveys shuddering or trembling.
James is making a devastating point.
Correct religious belief, by itself, is not the same thing as living, saving faith.
A person can acknowledge true facts about God without responding to Him in trusting allegiance.
A person can understand Christian doctrine while refusing the Christ that doctrine reveals.
A person can possess religious information without experiencing spiritual transformation.
But we must interpret James accurately.
James is not saying that demons possess genuine saving faith and simply lack enough good works to complete their salvation.
He is exposing the inadequacy of a claim to faith that produces no corresponding response.
Throughout James 2:14–26, he challenges the person who says he has faith but offers no evidence of it.
His question is whether that kind of claimed faith can save.
And he gives a striking example.
Someone sees a brother or sister lacking clothing and daily food.
They offer religious-sounding words.
They wish the person well.
But they do nothing to meet the need.
James asks what good that accomplishes.
Then comes his declaration in James 2:17:
“Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.” (KJV)
Dead faith.
Not weak faith that is crying out for help.
Not immature faith that still needs to grow.
Not a wounded Christian desperately learning how to obey.
But a profession of faith that remains empty of the life it claims to possess.
This matters because Scripture never presents good works as the price we pay to purchase forgiveness.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (KJV)
Salvation is God's gift.
Not your achievement.
Not your religious résumé.
Not the sum of your donations, church attendance, public prayers, or acts of service.
Christ's saving work is sufficient.
And yet Paul continues in Ephesians 2:10:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.” (KJV)
Do you see the order?
We are not saved because we have accumulated enough good works.
We are saved by grace through faith, and those who are made new in Christ are created for a life in which good works have their rightful place.
Obedience is not the purchase price of salvation.
It is a fitting fruit of a life being transformed by grace.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because when you confuse fruit with the root, you either become proud of your performance or terrified by your failures.
But when you understand the Gospel, you realize that Jesus is both the source of your salvation and the One who calls you into a new way of life.
He does not merely forgive your past.
He begins transforming your present.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God brings salvation and trains believers to reject ungodliness and live in a godly manner.
Grace is not indifferent to how we live.
Grace teaches us.
Grace corrects us.
Grace draws us away from what destroys us.
Grace brings us back to Jesus.
So what about the person who says:
“I believe Jesus is Lord, but I refuse to follow Him”?
We must distinguish what that person means.

If they mean, “I believe Jesus exists, but I have no intention of trusting Him, obeying Him, repenting of sin, or acknowledging His rightful authority over my life,” Scripture gives them no basis for assurance of salvation merely because they acknowledge certain facts about Christ.
Jesus' words in Luke 6:46 directly challenge that contradiction.
James 2 warns against empty professions of faith.
And Matthew 7:21–23 warns that even impressive religious activity does not guarantee a genuine relationship with Christ.
But if they mean, “I believe Jesus is Lord, and I want to follow Him, yet I keep failing, struggling, and discovering how weak I am,” that is a different conversation.
Such a person needs biblical encouragement, repentance where necessary, wise discipleship, and a deeper understanding of Christ's grace.
Not an automatic declaration that every struggle proves they are lost.
There is a world of difference between resisting temptation and embracing rebellion.
Between confessing sin and defending it.
Between stumbling on the road and declaring that you will never walk it.
Only God perfectly knows the human heart.
We cannot see every hidden motive or pronounce the final eternal destiny of a particular individual.
But we can take seriously what Jesus has revealed.
And His warnings are too important to soften into comfortable religious slogans.
Perhaps the most frightening form of spiritual deception is not openly rejecting Jesus.
Perhaps it is learning how to speak about Him so convincingly that you no longer notice how little room you have given Him in your actual life.
You can say Jesus is Lord on Sunday and treat His words as optional on Monday.
You can quote Scripture about forgiveness while refusing to forgive.
You can sing about holiness while privately defending the sin you know He is calling you to abandon.
You can post about surrender while making certain parts of your life permanently off-limits to God.
And because everyone around you sees the religious version of you, nobody asks the questions that your conscience has been trying to ask for years.
Until one night.
The room is quiet.
The phone is finally down.
There is no congregation to impress.
No worship music to create an atmosphere.
No audience.
Just you.
And the question you cannot escape.
If Jesus is truly my Lord, why have I been treating His commands as suggestions?
That moment can become a turning point.
Not because fear itself saves you.
Not because emotional intensity earns forgiveness.
But because the truth may finally bring you to honest repentance and renewed trust in Christ.
The Greek word often translated “repent” is μετανοέω (metanoeō).
It carries the sense of changing one's mind or thinking, and in the New Testament's call to repentance, that change is inseparable from turning toward God.
Repentance is not merely feeling bad because you were caught.
It is not simply crying during a sermon.
It is not promising to become perfect by tomorrow morning.
It is turning from sin toward God, acknowledging His truth, and responding to His mercy.
Jesus proclaimed in Mark 1:15:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.” (KJV)
Repent.
And believe.
Not repent so that you can become worthy of the Gospel.
Not believe so that you can continue treating sin as your master.
But turn to the Savior whose grace forgives and whose power makes new life possible.
And here is the beautiful part.
The very Jesus who warns against empty religious confession is the Jesus who welcomes repentant sinners.
He is not waiting for you to clean every stain from your soul before approaching Him.
You cannot wash away your own guilt.
That is why you need a Savior.
Consider the thief crucified beside Jesus in Luke 23.
He had no opportunity to build a long record of Christian service.
No opportunity to spend years attending church.
No opportunity to demonstrate decades of obedience.
He acknowledged his guilt and appealed to Jesus in faith.
And Jesus promised him paradise.
That scene demolishes the idea that salvation must be earned through a lifetime of religious achievement.
But it does not establish that genuine faith can knowingly reject Jesus' lordship.
The thief turned toward Christ with the opportunity he had.
His hope rested entirely on the mercy and authority of Jesus.
And Jesus was enough.
That is the Gospel.
A Savior sufficient for the guilty.
A King who receives the repentant.
A Redeemer who does not demand that broken people become their own rescuers.
The cross declares that sin is more serious than we want to admit.
The resurrection declares that Jesus is more powerful than death.
And grace declares that forgiveness is available to people who could never earn it.
This is why the message of salvation must never become either cheap permission to rebel or an exhausting demand to save ourselves.
Jesus Christ is not a decorative addition to an otherwise self-directed life.
He is Lord.
And His lordship is not bad news for the sinner who comes to Him.
It is good news.
Because the One who has rightful authority over your life is also the One who loved sinners enough to die for them.
The hands that call you to follow Him are the hands that were pierced.
The voice that commands repentance is the voice that cried, “It is finished.”
The Lord who confronts your sin is the Savior who offers forgiveness.
Think about that.
The One you have resisted is the One who offers to restore you.
The One whose commands you have ignored is the One who knows how deeply sin has wounded you.
The One who refuses to call darkness light is the One who can bring you into His marvelous light.
And perhaps the greatest tragedy would be spending your entire life defending the name of Jesus while refusing the grace that could actually change you.
So today, do not merely ask, “Do I believe Jesus is Lord?”
Ask something deeper.
“Am I trusting the Jesus I confess?”
“When His Word exposes my sin, do I defend myself endlessly, or am I willing to repent?”
“When I fail, do I run away from Christ, or do I return to Him?”
“Am I depending on His grace, or am I depending on my religious reputation?”
“Is there any area of my life where I have already decided that I will never obey Him?”
These are not questions for condemning every imperfect believer.
They are questions for honest self-examination.
Second Corinthians 13:5 calls professing Christians to examine themselves concerning the faith.
And examination is not the same as hopelessness.
Sometimes the most merciful thing God does is expose the false foundation we have been standing on.
Not to leave us in despair.
But to lead us to the only foundation that can hold.
Jesus Christ.
If this message has exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to manufacture a dramatic public confession to prove that you are sincere.
You can begin with an honest prayer.

“Lord Jesus, I have called You Lord while resisting Your Word. Forgive me. I cannot save myself, and I cannot transform my own heart. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Teach me to trust You, turn from sin, and follow You. Where I have been rebellious, bring me to repentance. Where I am weak, strengthen me. Where I am deceived, open my eyes. I do not want merely to know things about You. I want to know You. Amen.”
And if you are already following Jesus but feel exhausted by the battle against sin, hear this too.
Do not confuse conviction with rejection.
Do not confuse your weakness with the weakness of your Savior.
Do not imagine that Jesus is surprised by the wounds you bring before Him.
Keep coming to Christ.
Keep confessing sin.
Keep learning His Word.
Keep walking with faithful believers who will tell you the truth and help carry your burdens.
And when you fall, do not build a home in the place where you stumbled.
Return to Him.
Because sanctification is not accomplished by pretending you no longer need grace.
It is the continuing work of God in people who will always need their Savior.
And this is where the Gospel Warrior mission becomes deeply personal.
There are people scrolling through Facebook tonight who believe they are too sinful to return to God.
Others have spent years in church without ever understanding the difference between religious performance and genuine faith.
Some are struggling quietly.
Some are drifting.
Some are desperately trying to find their way back.
And some have never truly heard the Gospel explained without manipulation, condemnation, or false promises.
They need Scripture.
They need sound biblical teaching.
They need encouragement rooted in truth.
Most of all, they need to hear about Jesus Christ.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to sell salvation.

But to keep placing Christ-centered, Scripture-anchored teaching in front of people who may be one honest encounter with biblical truth away from repentance, renewed faith, or a deeper walk with Jesus.
If this article has helped you understand something you previously misunderstood, please do not let it disappear into your feed.
A simple share can place this message before someone who would never search for a sermon but might stop long enough to read a question that speaks directly to their soul.
There may come a day when you need to remember that salvation is by grace, that genuine faith matters, and that the Savior who calls you to follow Him is also the Savior who restores the fallen.
And I want to ask you something personal.
Not for a religious performance.
Not because a public comment can prove that you are saved.
But because sometimes putting an honest struggle into words can open the door to encouragement and prayer.
Have you been struggling to follow Jesus, or have you realized that you have been calling Him Lord while keeping parts of your life away from Him?
Someone reading your words may recognize their own story.
We want this community to be a place where Scripture is taken seriously, grace is never cheapened, repentance is never replaced by performance, and Jesus Christ remains at the center.
These resources are intended to help believers grow in biblical understanding, prayer, spiritual maturity, and faithful discipleship.
And if this ministry has genuinely helped you, I also want to extend a personal invitation.
Scripture teaches the importance of generosity and supporting Gospel work.
In 2 Corinthians 9:7, Paul writes:
That last part matters.
Not grudgingly.
Not out of necessity.
Christian giving must never be extracted through fear, guilt, or the suggestion that God's favor can be purchased.
Your sharing helps extend its reach.
And your prayers matter deeply.
It is simply a way to express appreciation for those who choose to stand with this ministry.
The greatest reason to support Gospel work, however, is not a discount or a product.
It is the opportunity to help make biblical truth accessible to people who need it.
The Gospel is not behind a paywall.
The free resources remain an invitation to grow.
And no one needs to pay to receive the forgiveness Jesus Christ offers.
Because the ultimate goal is not to build an audience that admires Gospel Warrior.
It is to point people toward the Lord Jesus Christ.
Can someone believe Jesus is Lord, refuse to follow Him, and still be saved?
The biblical answer requires us to distinguish intellectual acknowledgment from genuine saving faith.
A person who merely agrees that Jesus is Lord while deliberately rejecting Him has no biblical grounds to assume that such acknowledgment alone saves.
Romans 10:9 calls us to genuine faith in the risen Lord.
Luke 6:46 exposes the contradiction of calling Jesus Lord while refusing His words.
James 2:19 reminds us that even demons acknowledge true things about God.
Yet salvation remains entirely the gift of God's grace, received through faith in Jesus Christ—not a reward for flawless obedience.
Genuine faith does not make us perfect.
But it brings us into relationship with the Savior who forgives us and begins changing us.
That is why the answer is neither “Just believe the facts and live however you want” nor “Obey perfectly or Jesus will reject you.”
The answer is Christ Himself.
Trust Him.
Come to Him.
Repent.
Receive His grace.
And follow Him—not to earn His love, but because the Savior who loved you and gave Himself for you is worthy of your life.
You may have arrived at this article thinking the greatest question was whether someone could be saved without following Jesus.
But perhaps the question you needed most was far more personal.
Have I been following Jesus… or have I only been following the version of Christianity that allows me to remain in control?
There is still grace for the person willing to stop pretending.
There is still forgiveness for the sinner who turns to Christ.
There is still hope for the believer who has fallen.
And there is still a Savior whose mercy is greater than the shame you have carried.
Do not mistake His patience for permission to remain unchanged.
And do not mistake His call to repentance for a refusal to receive you.
Come to Jesus.
Not merely to the idea of Jesus.
Not merely to the culture of Christianity.
Not merely to a religious identity.
Come to the crucified and risen Lord.
Because the most beautiful testimony is not that you spent your entire life calling Him Lord.
It is that, by His grace, you came to trust Him as Lord—and discovered that the One you feared surrendering to was the very One who could set you free.
The greatest tragedy is not that Jesus knows every scandal in your story—it is to spend your life hiding from the very grace that could rewrite it.
